article.overview: A dust detector measures dust grains in the space environment, either by recording individual grain impacts or by measuring the cumulative response of many small grains. Two different lunar dust detectors are documented in the sources accessed for this version. The first is the Lunar Dust Experiment (LDEX) on NASA's LADEE mission, an impact ionisation detector that operated in lunar orbit [1][2][3]. The second is the Apollo Dust, Thermal and Radiation Engineering Measurements (DTREM) package, also called the Apollo Dust Detector, which the Apollo 11, 12, 14 and 15 crews emplaced on the lunar surface to measure how dust, thermal cycling and radiation changed the output of exposed solar cells [5][6]. The two instruments answer different questions and should not be compared as if they were the same design.
article.description:
A dust detector is a particle sensor built for the space environment. Instruments in this class use one of three broad approaches. Impact detectors register individual grains that strike a sensing surface and infer grain mass and speed from the signal, subject to calibration [1][2]. Charge-integration detectors sum the signal from many grains that are too small to be detected one at a time [2][3]. Surface accumulation monitors, such as the Apollo DTREM, do not count grains. They track how the output of exposed solar cells changes as dust, thermal cycling and radiation act on them [5][6].

LDEX uses impact ionisation: a grain striking a hemispherical target creates a plasma cloud, and the electrons and ions from that cloud are separated by electric fields and read out as electrical pulses [2]. The SIS states that LDEX's design is based on earlier impact-ionisation dust instruments flown on Heos 2, Galileo, Ulysses and Cassini [2]. A dust detector is therefore a specialised sensor rather than a camera or a sample collector. It reports the impacts it records, and calibration determines how those impacts are converted into grain properties.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The primary purpose of a lunar dust detector is to determine how much dust is present near the Moon, how large the grains are, and how the population varies with position and time. For LDEX, the SIS describes the scientific goal as weighing two competing dust sources against each other: ejecta produced when interplanetary micrometeoroids strike the Moon, and small grains lofted from the surface by plasma-induced near-surface electric fields [2]. The SIS design also includes measurement of a collective current from grains below the individual-detection threshold [2].

The Apollo DTREM had a different purpose: to determine the effects of lunar and meteoric dust, thermal stresses and radiation exposure on solar cells [5]. Its data bear on the long-term surface environment relevant to solar power, but the sources accessed here do not quantify a dust flux or deposition rate from it. A NASA-credited press caption describes the Apollo 12 unit as having made the first measurement of lunar dust accumulation [6]. That caption is not independently quantified in the sources accessed.
article.operating_principle:
Impact ionisation (LDEX). A dust grain strikes a hemispherical target and generates a plasma cloud. A bias on an ion-focusing grid separates electrons from ions. Electrons are collected on the target, and ions are detected by a microchannel plate (MCP) behind the grid [2]. An impact whose signal exceeds a user-defined threshold triggers recording of target and MCP waveforms. The impact charge is measured on both channels, and the grain's mass is calculated from that charge using laboratory calibration [2].

The specification gives a mass calibration for nominal conditions: 1.67 km/s impact speed, 20 °C, an 850 V MCP bias and a 2.54 cm radial position. It gives mi = qi × (2.88 ± 0.3)×10⁻³ kg for the ion channel and me = qe × (0.736 ± 0.075) kg for the electron channel, with a charge-to-mass ratio of about 1.36 C/kg [2]. The SIS footnotes these coefficients as pending final calibration analysis. They are calibration values from the instrument specification, not measurements of a lunar dust population.

Charge-integration mode (LDEX). For grains below the individual-detection threshold, LDEX integrates the MCP signal to measure collective current [2][3]. The background, such as ultraviolet light and energetic particles, is measured every 10 s by switching the ion-focusing grid to +30 V, which rejects impact plasma ions and records the background signal [2].

Photovoltaic accumulation (Apollo DTREM). The package has three solar cells and three thermistors. The Apollo 11, 14 and 15 units had three cells mounted on top of the box facing upwards: one with a cover glass, one exposed directly to space, and one pre-irradiated before mounting. The Apollo 12 unit had three identical cells, facing east, west and up [5]. The DTREM cycled through its six sensors and transmitted a set of measurements about every 54 seconds. Most of the information depends on relative changes in each cell's output rather than absolute values in millivolts, according to the restoration team [5].
article.scientific_importance: Direct impact measurements can give grain mass and speed, subject to calibration [2]. The two dust sources that LDEX was designed to weigh against each other, micrometeoroid ejecta and surface-lofted grains, are competing explanations for the lunar dust environment, so a measurement that distinguishes them has scientific value [2]. Orbital and surface measurements answer different questions. LDEX sampled the dust encountered along a spacecraft's orbit around the Moon, so determining the source of that dust requires comparisons over time and position [2]. The DTREM record spans several years on the surface, and the restoration team described it as useful for investigating the long-term effects of the dust, thermal and radiation environment on the Moon [5]. The scientific value of a dust detector therefore depends on its calibration, its coverage in space and time, and whether its data can distinguish between dust sources.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a dust detector, because instruments differ by sensing principle, platform and calibration. The two examples below describe one orbital impact detector and one surface solar-cell monitor. Neither instrument's mass, dimensions, power or sensor area is publicly specified in the sources accessed for this version, and this article does not infer them. The article therefore presents no comparative figures.

examples.name: Lunar Dust Experiment (LDEX), NASA LADEE
examples.status: Flown and operated in lunar orbit on NASA's LADEE mission. The SIS describes commissioning and science phases and a PDS archive of LDEX data. The end-of-mission status is not described in the sources accessed.
examples.sensor_area: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.sensing_principle: Impact ionisation for individual grains, plus collective current for smaller grains.
examples.threshold_status: The two threshold values conflict and have not been reconciled. Neither is adopted as the single figure.
examples.smaller_grain_search: Grains with radius around 0.1 um over the terminators, using the collective current, according to the NMSU page.
examples.operating_modes: ON or OFF only, according to the NMSU page.
examples.orbit_altitude_km: 30-100 above the lunar surface, according to the SIS.
examples.qualification: Values are taken from the LADEE LDEX PDS specification and NMSU-hosted data page. The mass calibration coefficients are pending final calibration analysis.

examples.name: Apollo Dust, Thermal and Radiation Engineering Measurements (DTREM) package (Apollo Dust Detector)
examples.type: Flown lunar-surface solar-cell dust accumulation monitor
examples.status: Flown and operated on the lunar surface. The Apollo 11 unit operated for a few months after emplacement in July 1969. The Apollo 12, 14 and 15 units operated from deployment until ALSEP shutdown in September 1977.
examples.sensor_configuration: Three solar cells and three thermistors on a small box. Apollo 11, 14 and 15: three cells facing upwards, one with a cover glass, one exposed directly to space, one pre-irradiated with a cover glass. Apollo 12: three identical cells facing east, west and up. Thermistors: one on the outside of the west-facing wall, one inside that wall and one beneath the solar cells.
examples.mounting: Apollo 12, 14 and 15 units were mounted on the top northwest corner of the ALSEP central station sunshield. The Apollo 11 unit was part of the Early Apollo Surface Experiments Package (EASEP).
examples.sampling: Cycled through six sensors and transmitted every 54.34 seconds.
examples.telemetry: Carried in the central station housekeeping (Word 33) telemetry as counts from 0 to 255.
examples.restoration_status_2012: Apollo 14 and 15 data were being converted to calibrated voltages and temperatures using translation tables from calibrated microfilm. Apollo 12 data were planned for initial release in raw count format.
examples.size_description: Described as matchbox-sized in a NASA-credited press caption for the Apollo 12 unit. No dimensions verified.
examples.qualification: A mass figure that appeared only in a secondary search snippet was not verified and is not adopted.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The LDEX dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources accessed. The DTREM package is described as a small box carrying three solar cells and three thermistors, with a matchbox-sized description given in a press caption for the Apollo 12 unit. No dimensions are verified for either instrument, so the two designs are not compared numerically.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No mass is verified for LDEX or the Apollo DTREM package in the sources accessed. The SIS gives mass calibration coefficients for converting charge to grain mass, which are not instrument mass figures. For spacecraft engineering, mass is normally expressed in kilograms, and it affects launch requirements, lander capacity, structural support and deployment design.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power for LDEX and for the Apollo DTREM package is not verified in the sources accessed. The LDEX SIS lists commanding of an aperture cover and an autonomous sun-safing enable state, but gives no power figure in the text examined.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
A dust detector in lunar orbit operates in a near-vacuum and in a background of ultraviolet light, energetic particles and solar wind. LDEX's grid configuration and background-subtraction cycle are part of its response to that environment. The mass calibration is quoted at 20 °C and an 850 V MCP bias, and the calibration was carried out over an MCP bias range of 680 to 940 V. The SIS lists telemetry items for an arm-cover command and an autonomous sun-safing enable state, so the aperture cover and sun-safing function are commanded and monitored through the spacecraft.

A dust detector on the surface faces different conditions, including lunar day-night thermal cycling and dust settling on its sensing surface. The DTREM record shows effects of this kind: according to the restoration team, the solar-cell outputs show signatures of sunrise, sunset, eclipses, lunar module ascent, and long-term dust deposition and thermal and radiation damage. The sources accessed do not separate these contributions quantitatively.
article.limitations: Grains below the individual-detection threshold are counted only through a collective current, so their individual sizes and masses are not measured. Mass and size depend on laboratory calibration at a specified impact speed, temperature and MCP bias, and the SIS states that the mass coefficients are pending final calibration analysis. Integrated mass requires assumed grain sizes, which the SIS leaves to higher-level processing. The SIS and the NMSU-hosted data page give different individual-grain thresholds. The effective sensing area increases with radial distance while detection efficiency falls slightly, so the calibration position matters. An orbiting detector measures only the dust encountered along its own orbit. The DTREM solar-cell outputs reflect some combination of dust, radiation and thermal effects that the sources accessed do not separate. The DTREM Apollo 12 data were planned for initial release in raw counts, and a final calibrated release is not shown in the sources accessed.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A dust detector can be carried as an orbiter instrument or as part of a surface payload. LDEX was an orbiter instrument, and the Apollo DTREM was a surface package emplaced by crews. The orbiter pathway is described first, followed by the surface pathway as documented for Apollo.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into the spacecraft on Earth, including its aperture cover and commanding interfaces (LDEX).
Launch the spacecraft and transfer it to the Moon (LDEX).
Enter lunar orbit at an operational altitude of 30-100 km above the surface, according to the SIS (LDEX).
Commission the instrument, following the commissioning and science phases described in the SIS (LDEX).
Operate the instrument through spacecraft commands and telemetry, including sun-safing (LDEX).
Deliver the calibrated data to the Planetary Data System (LDEX).

Crews emplaced the Apollo 11, 12, 14 and 15 packages on the lunar surface; the Apollo 12, 14 and 15 units were mounted on the ALSEP central station (Apollo DTREM). Transfer hardware, lander and step-by-step emplacement are not described in the sources accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: LDEX was deployed as an orbiter instrument on the LADEE spacecraft. The Apollo DTREM packages were emplaced by the crews of Apollo 11, 12, 14 and 15. A future surface instrument would be integrated on Earth, carried to the Moon by a lander or rover, placed on the surface, and connected to power and data. Its mounting and interfaces are not verified for any specific system.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: LADEE carried LDEX in lunar orbit. The Apollo 11, 12, 14 and 15 crews placed DTREM packages on the lunar surface, with the Apollo 12, 14 and 15 units on the ALSEP central station.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted. Any new dust detector would need verified mass, power, mounting and interface data before compatibility could be assessed.

article.historical_significance:
LDEX is the best-documented flown impact dust detector in this article. The SIS states that the instrument was built and tested at LASP and calibrated at the Colorado Center for Lunar Dust and Atmospheric Studies. Its design derives from earlier impact-ionisation dust instruments flown on Heos 2, Galileo, Ulysses and Cassini.

The Apollo DTREM units are the earliest surface examples in this article. A NASA-credited press caption describes the Apollo 12 unit as making the first measurement of lunar dust accumulation. The units operated on the surface for up to nearly eight years. The 2012 restoration work, carried out by the Lunar Data Node at NSSDC, aimed to make their data available to researchers worldwide for the first time once restored.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: This article rests on two flown instruments with different designs and different evidence bases. LDEX is documented through a PDS specification [2], a PDS data page [3] and a dataset DOI [4]. The Apollo DTREM is documented through a 2012 restoration paper [5] and a press caption [6]. The LDEX threshold values conflict between the SIS and the NMSU data page, and the SIS mass calibration is pending final calibration analysis [2][3]. Sensor area, mass and power remain unresolved for LDEX [2][3]. The instrument paper by Horányi et al. (2014) [1] was not accessed in full for this version, so its citation is used only for bibliographic identity. The orbital altitude is taken from the SIS, which gives 30–100 km; other altitude values were not re-checked for this version. The DTREM mass, dimensions and power were not verified, and a mass figure from a secondary search snippet is not adopted. The DTREM restoration status is described as of 2012, and a final calibrated release was not verified. No direct image asset was verified for either instrument. Two further sensor concepts that appeared in secondary search results, including a particle impact event sensor, were not verified and are not described. The generic description of surface dust detectors is an engineering framing and not a certified design specification.
